rationale: Reserve balances are paid by Federal Reserve Banks and administered as a monetary-policy tool; treat as money for eligible bank holder surface.
NY Fed states ON RRP uses Treasury securities, eligible counterparties include primary dealers, banks, MMFs and GSEs; eligibility is restricted and operationally gated.
Close to ON RRP, but restricted to foreign/international monetary authority arrangements and not generally transferable to private holders.
Bills have minimal duration risk and very high funding convertibility; Treasury repo data and collateral schedules support near-cash treatment.

Treasury coupons are deeply repo-able but not price-invariant; upgrade from owner 0.65 because collateral schedules show 95-99% margins by duration, while duration volatility prevents bill-like weight.
Checkable deposits are the anchor par claim in the diagnostic; no haircut applied.
Reg D’s numeric transfer limit was deleted, but institutions are not required to suspend limits and reservation-of-right terms remain, so savings/MMDA are slightly below checkable.
Evidence supports collateral eligibility for CDs, but household time-deposit access frictions vary by contract; remains assumption-grade.

SEC removed temporary redemption gates and liquidity-threshold fee tie, raised daily/weekly liquidity requirements, but institutional prime/tax-exempt funds can face mandatory liquidity fees over 5% daily net redemptions.
Short private money-market instruments are collateralizable and short-duration but carry issuer/rollover stress risk.
Outstanding mortgage loans are not money for household borrowers; for lender assets, collateral value is institution-specific and not broadly repo-convertible.
Lower duration does not make the outstanding loan balance a household liquid buffer.
If the future channel wants borrower liquidity from undrawn HELOC lines, that is a separate commitment object, not the balance stock.
A revolving balance is not money-like for the borrower; ABS/receivable financing is not enough to treat the balance as borrower buffer.
Low liquidity service; collateral schedules for ABS do not create household money.
Federal student loan balance is not a liquid buffer; any pledge value is lender/institution specific.
Private student loan balance is not a liquid buffer; keep low.
No market moneyness; lender collateralization is not borrower convertibility.
C&I loans can have collateral value to banks but are not generally a transferable money substitute.
Syndicated loans have some marketability but do not have clean repo/deposit-like convertibility.
Official collateral margins are high for IG bonds, but corporate spread/convenience-yield literature shows Treasuries carry special liquidity/safety premia over corporates.
Munis receive 90-98% margin by rating/duration in official schedules, but market depth/access is weaker than Treasuries; no direct repo universalization.
Agency MBS have high official collateral margins and are eligible in Fed repo operations, but prepayment and duration risk make them less money-like than Treasuries.

Fixed CRE mortgages are even less money-like during rate stress.
BNPL outstanding balance is not money-like; any securitization liquidity belongs to provider/funder balance sheet.
Deposit float is money-like in this diagnostic.
MMF float inherits MMF redemption/access and liquidity-fee rules.
Outstanding card float is not borrower liquidity; keep in low bucket.
Funding liability is a financing object
column9: not a liquid buffer; small collateral/funding recognition only.
